ideas.title: Show starvation and steps per game
ideas.what: Add a panel to the test results that shows, for each agent, the share of test games that ended by starving or crashing, next to the mean steps per game.
ideas.why: The GA's 1,937 steps per test game suggests it loops until it starves, but the current table does not show how games ended, so the learner has to infer looping from one number.
ideas.expected: Makes reward hacking like the survival-driven wandering visible in one glance, so learners can spot it in any run.

ideas.title: Compare agents on equal compute
ideas.what: Offer a budget mode that gives each agent the same number of CPU cores (or the same environment steps) instead of the same wall-clock time, and report the resulting comparison.
ideas.why: The GA used 11 cores at about 255k steps per second, while DQN used one core at about 2.3k steps per second; a 10-minute race is therefore not a fair comparison of learning methods.
ideas.expected: Would show whether DQN's lead holds when both agents have the same resources, rather than depending on hardware assignment.

ideas.title: Compare several seeds with spread
ideas.what: Run one recipe across several seeds and show the test mean for each agent as a range or error bar, so a difference is only called real when the spread does not overlap.
ideas.why: This run's headline rests on one seed, and the GA's 15.99 versus 33.95 gap could be partly luck; the DQN change of +0.94 is clearly noise but the dashboard cannot show that today.
ideas.expected: Lets learners judge whether a change is real, for example by requiring a gap larger than the seed-to-seed spread, which should prevent most misreadings of one-seed runs.

ideas.title: Store test-game steps for every run
ideas.what: Record mean steps per test game and mean steps per run for every run, including older ones, so the lesson's comparisons can be checked from the record.
ideas.why: The scratch run's wandering claim (1,937 steps per test game) cannot be checked because that run has no test-game statistics, though this run shows the metric is useful (543 steps for the GA, 236 for DQN).
ideas.expected: Makes every 'the snake wanders' claim verifiable from the record, so comparisons between lessons use the same measured numbers.

ideas.title: Seed-group spread on test scores
ideas.what: Show the test mean with its spread (min, max, or standard deviation) across several seeds of the same recipe on the results table, so a single seed cannot be read as a ranking.
ideas.why: The GA and DQN test means differ by about 4 points on one seed, and the training curves wobble by 4 to 5 points between checkpoints, so the lab cannot tell noise from effect here.
ideas.expected: Lets learners see whether a gap is bigger than the seed-to-seed spread, which is usually a few points for these runs.

ideas.title: DQN train-every-N-steps setting
ideas.what: Add a setting for how often DQN takes a gradient update (for example one update per 4 environment steps), so the agent can spend less time training and more time collecting experience per second.
ideas.why: DQN ran at about 1.3k steps per second and collected only 391k steps in 5 minutes, while the GA collected 30.8M. Its curve was still rising at minute 1.4 and then flattened, so more experience per minute may help it.
ideas.expected: Several times more environment steps per minute for DQN, which could raise its test mean by a few points within the same 5-minute budget.

ideas.title: Free-space flood-fill vision feature
ideas.what: Add a vision input that reports how many empty squares the snake can reach from its head without crossing its body or a wall, perhaps split into the left, straight and right options. This gives the network a direct sense of boxing itself in.
ideas.why: Both the window and rays visions still show DQN dying from its own body in 69 to 76% of test games, even though each sees the nearby body. Neither reports how much room is left, which is what matters when the snake grows long on a small board.
ideas.expected: DQN's body-crash share falls by 10 points or more (from 69% to 60% or lower), and its test mean rises by 3 or more points.

ideas.title: Separate penalties for body and wall crashes
ideas.what: Add two reward features, one for crashing into the body and one for crashing into a wall, so each crash type can be weighted separately instead of sharing one death penalty.
ideas.why: Raising the single death penalty cut body crashes from 69% to 56% but raised wall crashes from 31% to 44%, showing one penalty cannot target both failure modes.
ideas.expected: A body-only penalty should cut body crashes without pushing wall crashes up; the target is a body share under 50% with the test mean above 28.

ideas.title: Run several seeds and show spread
ideas.what: Add a button that trains the same recipe with three or four seeds and reports the test mean with its range (or standard error) on the dashboard and in the lesson table.
ideas.why: This run's key result (DQN up 3.9 points) rests on a single seed, and the lab currently has no way to measure seed-to-seed spread without launching each seed by hand.
ideas.expected: Each comparison would come with an error bar, so learners could tell differences larger than seed noise from smaller ones, instead of guessing.

ideas.title: Show crash mix over training
ideas.what: Plot the share of wall, body, starved and won endings in each evaluation, rather than only in the final test table.
ideas.why: The gamma change moved the crash mix (body 56% to 29%, wall 44% to 71%) while the test mean moved less. The current view shows only the end state, so learners cannot see when the shift happened.
ideas.expected: Learners could see whether the crash mix shifts early in training or only late, which would help explain how the horizon works.

ideas.title: Show how game endings change over training
ideas.what: Plot the share of wall, body, starved and won games at each training checkpoint, not only at the final test.
ideas.why: The GA's 22 starved games are visible only in the final test table. The curves do not show when looping began or whether it is growing.
ideas.expected: Lets the learner see whether the starved share rises during training, for example from 0% to 22%, and link it to the reward changes.

ideas.title: Add a reachable-space vision feature
ideas.what: Add an input that reports how many empty squares the snake could still reach from its head, using a flood fill that stops at walls and body.
ideas.why: DQN with short vision dies in its own body in 88% of test games, and it plateaus at about 15-16 in training. The catalog's visions do not show the snake how much room it has left.
ideas.expected: Reduces DQN's body-collision share below 60% and lifts its test mean by 5 or more points at 3 minutes, if the room count is what limits it.

ideas.title: Score per CPU core-minute in comparisons
ideas.what: Add a comparison view that shows test score divided by the CPU cores each agent used and the minutes it ran, next to the existing score per env step.
ideas.why: The GA ran on 11 cores while DQN ran on 1, so a same-wall-clock comparison favours the GA. Its 66 million env steps against DQN's 0.26 million mostly reflect hardware, not learning quality.
ideas.expected: Lets learners see whether DQN's per-step efficiency (score 15 after 110k steps) beats the GA on a fair compute basis, which the current table cannot show.

ideas.title: Convolutional network for full-board vision
ideas.what: Add a network that scans the board with shared small filters, so it learns local patterns (such as 'body is one square ahead') once instead of separately for each of 1083 inputs. It would be used for both the GA and DQN.
ideas.why: The full view gives the GA 1083 inputs, and it starved in all 100 test games with 50M steps and a flat curve. The DQN reached 30 with the same view, but its training was slow at about 100 to 750 steps per second.
ideas.expected: The GA could move well above its current mean of 1.44 with the full board, and the DQN could train faster per step, reaching the 20-plus plateau in fewer environment steps.

ideas.title: Plot greedy test scores on the learning curves
ideas.what: Draw the greedy evaluation score that DQN already computes every eval_every steps as a line on its learning curve, next to the training mean. Show the evaluation points so a learner can see when the saved best model improved.
ideas.why: The training mean (23.0 for DQN, 21.2 for GA) understates the test score (37.56 and 36.27), and the curves stop around 21 to 23 while the saved model keeps improving. The current curves cannot show which model is being saved, so a learner cannot tell whether a plateau is real.
ideas.expected: Learners can see the gap between training mean and greedy score at every checkpoint, and can spot plateaus or late gains. This makes the minute-by-minute comparison fair and reduces guesses about when to stop a run.

ideas.title: Crash-type share over training
ideas.what: Plot the wall, body, starved and won shares of training games against env steps, so learners can see when a snake starts avoiding walls and whether its deaths move to the body.
ideas.why: The test table shows the crash shift only at the end. The training curves show a single mean, so we cannot tell whether the wall share fell gradually or changed suddenly.
ideas.expected: Makes the moment the wall share falls visible in each run, e.g. the shift in this run should appear by about minute 3 to 5 if it tracks the learning curve.

ideas.title: Growing penalty for long gaps without eating
ideas.what: A reward feature that subtracts a small amount each move, increasing with the number of moves since the last apple, so loops become more costly the longer they last. It would replace the flat per-move hunger cost with one that targets wandering specifically.
ideas.why: 66 of 100 test games starved after 652 steps with 46 steps per apple, and the existing hunger term is flat, so it does not single out long loops.
ideas.expected: Starved games fall below 20 out of 100 and steps per apple fall below 30, while the test mean stays at or above the level without hunger.

ideas.title: Flag CPU throttling on the training curve
ideas.what: Mark the points on the curve where the machine is on battery or throttling, and show steps per second next to generations so a slowdown is not read as a learning change.
ideas.why: Steps per second fell from about 170k to about 55k after 2.2 minutes while the machine was on battery, and the training mean changed at the same time.
ideas.expected: Learners can tell a compute drop from a learning plateau, so they will not misread late-run curves.

ideas.title: Warn when the machine is on battery
ideas.what: Show a warning on the run page when the machine is on battery, and display the steps per second next to each run's expected range for its algorithm and inputs, so slow runs are flagged before they are compared.
ideas.why: This run ran at about 59k steps per second, while comparable 3-game GA runs managed 220k to 300k. Its generation count and score are therefore hard to compare with other runs, and nothing on the page explained why.
ideas.expected: Learners would see slowdowns at a glance, which would avoid misreading generation counts as a measure of the algorithm.

ideas.title: Check the GA's training mean scale
ideas.what: Verify how the GA's mean_last_100 is computed and make it match the test score's units (or label it clearly), so the training curve can be compared with the test mean.
ideas.why: The logged GA training mean ended at 0.56, while the best game was 33 and the test mean was 22. The prediction and the lesson's note both assumed a training mean of 15 or more, so the curve as logged cannot be read against the test score.
ideas.expected: Training and test scores would be directly comparable, letting learners judge overfitting and the late-decline question from the curve alone.

ideas.title: Show the GA's champion score next to the population mean
ideas.what: Add a curve of the best genome's score on a fixed evaluation set, plotted beside the population's training mean, with both labelled in apples as well as reward units.
ideas.why: This run's training mean (7.79) and test mean (39.07) are on very different scales, which makes it hard to tell whether training is still improving.
ideas.expected: Learners can read progress from one curve; the gap between the champion curve and the population mean would show how much luck contributes to the training numbers.

ideas.title: Flag comparisons that differ in several settings
ideas.what: When a run is compared to a baseline, list every recipe field that differs and warn when more than one changed.
ideas.why: The games-per-genome comparison here differs from its 10-game partner in tournament, mutation rate, starve penalty, and death split, so the lesson's answer is confounded.
ideas.expected: Learners catch confounded comparisons before drawing conclusions, which should reduce wrong attributions across lessons.

ideas.title: Compare agents on score per env step
ideas.what: A dashboard view that plots test score against env steps (log scale) and against wall-clock minutes for all agents on one chart, with seed-group bands.
ideas.why: The GA ran about 264M env steps and DQN about 2M in the same 10 minutes. The current curves mix the two units, making it hard to see that DQN is far more step-efficient while the GA is far faster per minute.
ideas.expected: A learner can read sample efficiency (DQN about 10x better per step at this stage) and speed (GA about 130x more steps per second) in one picture.

ideas.title: Compare seed groups at matched env steps
ideas.what: Report each run's test score at fixed env-step checkpoints (for example 250k, 500k, 1M) and show the seed-group mean and spread at each one, so early learning speed can be compared directly.
ideas.why: This run's curve rises fast in the first minute, but the record holds only the final stats for the no-hint runs, so the claim that hints speed up early learning cannot be tested from what is stored.
ideas.expected: A fair sample-efficiency comparison for the hint question; it should show whether the hint changes score at 250k steps even if the final score does not change.

ideas.title: Plot curves against env steps at fine resolution
ideas.what: Log the training mean at regular env-step intervals, such as every 50k steps, and plot all hint variants on the same step axis. Show the first 500k steps by default.
ideas.why: This run's curve has one point at 0.02 min and the next at 0.92 min, so the lesson's question about which hint helps most early cannot be answered from the curves.
ideas.expected: Lets learners compare how many steps each hint needs to reach a mean of 10, which is the early speed-up the lesson asks about.

ideas.title: Early-learning speed score per run
ideas.what: Report the average training score over the first few minutes, or the environment steps needed to reach a set score, for each run. Show it next to the final test score in seed-group comparisons.
ideas.why: The lesson asks which hint helps most early on, but the final test scores differ by less than the seed spread, and the early comparison needs one number per run. This run's curve shows the plateau is reached within about one minute, so the early phase is where hints would matter.
ideas.expected: Would separate hint groups by learning speed, for example showing whether a hint reaches a training mean of 15 in fewer env steps, and makes the early-phase comparison readable without eyeballing curves.

ideas.title: Final exploration floor for DQN
ideas.what: Add a setting for the exploration rate the DQN keeps at the end of training (for example 0.02), so the training mean is measured with less random play. Only the decay schedule is currently exposed.
ideas.why: The DQN's training mean plateaus at 19 to 20 while its greedy test score is about 26. Part of that gap is random moves in training games, which makes the training curve hard to read.
ideas.expected: The training mean should move closer to the test score (within about 2 to 3 points), so the curves become more useful for judging progress.

ideas.title: Report test results by seed as a spread
ideas.what: On the seed-group view, show each seed's test mean and game-ending mix as a small chart next to the group mean, with the spread shown as error bars.
ideas.why: The GA's group mean (29.3) hides one seed that starved in 36% of games and two that did not starve at all. A reader can miss that without opening each run.
ideas.expected: Readers see weak seeds and failure modes at a glance, so fewer conclusions rest on one seed.

ideas.title: Plot learning curves against env steps
ideas.what: Add a view that plots each algorithm's test or training score against env steps as well as wall-clock minutes, so sample efficiency can be seen directly.
ideas.why: The GA took about 80M env steps in 10 minutes and DQN about 1.2M. Under equal wall-clock time the comparison hides how much more per step DQN learns.
ideas.expected: Makes the sample-efficiency gap visible at a glance. Teaching value rather than a score change.

ideas.title: Convolutional network for the whole board
ideas.what: Add a network option that reads the full-board pictures with convolutional layers, which share weights across neighbouring squares, instead of one fully connected layer over 1,083 inputs.
ideas.why: DQN ran at only about 600 steps per second on whole-board inputs and got about 363,000 steps in 10 minutes. Its plateau suggests it has to relearn that nearby squares are related. The GA also needs to mutate about 17,000 weights.
ideas.expected: Several times more steps per second and a higher DQN plateau (over 35 in 10 minutes), without the GA slowdown.

ideas.title: Warn when a comparison changes several settings
ideas.what: When two runs in a lesson differ in more than the setting under test (here reward, time and vision), show a clear diff with a warning that the comparison is confounded.
ideas.why: This run's note says only vision changed from the rays-4 run, yet its reward (score only) and time (10 minutes) differ from that run's reward (with potential and hunger) and its 5-minute budget. That confound made the GA result hard to attribute.
ideas.expected: Fewer misread comparisons: learners would see the reward or time difference before drawing a conclusion from the vision change.

ideas.title: Show greedy test score on DQN's training curve
ideas.what: Plot the greedy evaluation score (the same score used for the saved model) alongside DQN's training mean, so the learner can see the policy's progress without exploration noise.
ideas.why: DQN's training mean stayed flat at about 21 from 1 to 10 minutes, while its greedy test score was about 38. The curve as drawn suggests DQN had stopped learning, which is misleading.
ideas.expected: Makes the training curve match the test score, avoiding the apparent plateau; no change to the agent.

ideas.title: Paired seed-difference view
ideas.what: Show, for each seed, the difference between two recipes next to the spread band of each group. The view would make a consistent but small gap visible as a single chart.
ideas.why: The four same-seed differences here are all positive (+0.7 to +5.2), but the two groups still overlap. The current view makes it hard to see how that pattern compares with the noise.
ideas.expected: Learners see whether a gap is consistent across seeds and how large it is relative to the spread, rather than comparing one best run with one worst run.

ideas.title: Log full-board games during training
ideas.what: Count how many training games fill the board, per generation for the GA and per episode for DQN, and plot that count on the curve.
ideas.why: The GA's best game reached 97 apples from about generation 212 onward, yet this seed won only 1 test game. The current logs cannot show how often the bonus actually fires during training.
ideas.expected: A direct measure of how often a win bonus is reached during training, so learners can check the 'almost never' claim against data.

ideas.title: Paired seed comparison with an interval
ideas.what: When two seed groups are compared, show the per-seed paired differences, their mean, and a rough 95% interval, with a plain note when the interval includes zero.
ideas.why: The bonus group looked better than baseline in its best run, but its paired mean difference (+1.8, paired t≈1.4 over 5 seeds) is consistent with zero, and the dashboard shows only the ranges.
ideas.expected: Learners would reach the correct 'no real difference' conclusion without hand-computing statistics; the bonus comparison would show a 95% interval of roughly −1 to +5 apples.

ideas.title: Count how often each reward fires
ideas.what: In the test summary, report how many test games triggered each reward feature (win, starve, death) alongside the ended counts.
ideas.why: The win bonus fired in only 2 of 500 bonus test games, and the learner had to infer its rarity from the ended table; a direct count would show at once whether a reward can matter.
ideas.expected: A learner could tell in seconds that a reward with a count of 2 cannot explain a difference of several apples.

ideas.title: Mutation rate that decays over generations
ideas.what: Start the GA with a high mutation rate for broad search, then lower it as generations pass, so late generations refine the kept networks. It would be a schedule that the trainer applies each generation.
ideas.why: The kept-network curve was still climbing at 10 minutes, and population_mean rose only from 16 to 29 over the last 5 minutes. A fixed mutation rate cannot be right at both the start and the end of training.
ideas.expected: A higher test mean at the same 10-minute budget, for example 5 or more points above a fixed 0.1 rate, though this would need several seeds to confirm.

ideas.title: Show seed-group differences with a noise band
ideas.what: In the seed-group view, show each recipe's mean test score as a bar with a ±1 standard deviation range across its seeds, and mark a difference as 'inside noise' when the bars overlap.
ideas.why: Here the mutation 0.05 vs 0.1 difference (about 5 points) sits inside the seed spread (9 points), and a learner reading single numbers could draw the wrong conclusion. The current view does not make this obvious.
ideas.expected: Learners stop reading differences smaller than the seed spread as real effects, and fewer conclusions flip when a run is repeated with a new seed.

ideas.title: Confidence intervals on seed-group comparisons
ideas.what: Show, for each seed group, the mean test score with an interval based on the spread across seeds, and mark whether two groups overlap, so a learner sees at once that a difference is within noise.
ideas.why: Three seeds per group gave standard deviations of 3.7 to 9 points, and the lesson's question could not be answered from the means alone.
ideas.expected: Learners stop reading differences under about 5 points as results; comparisons of this size would be flagged as inconclusive instead of being ranked.

ideas.title: Test score on the learning curve
ideas.what: Run the greedy test (no exploration, fixed seeds) at regular points during training and plot the score on the learning curve for both agents, next to the training mean.
ideas.why: DQN's training mean sits at about 16.9 while its final test score is 20.4, and the GA's training mean (51.2) and test score (50.7) nearly match. The curves do not show when DQN's best test score was reached, or whether its test score also plateaued after one minute.
ideas.expected: Learners could see whether DQN's test score plateaus as early as its training mean does, and whether the saved best model came from the early or late part of the run.

ideas.title: Death causes over the training curve
ideas.what: Plot the share of wall, body and starvation deaths in each training checkpoint, not only in the final test games.
ideas.why: Body collisions are 82% of DQN's and 90% of the GA's test games, but the run only reports them at the end. We cannot tell whether crashes into the body grew as the snake got longer or were already common early on.
ideas.expected: Shows whether the body-crash share rises with snake length during training, which would confirm the self-trap explanation and make the room and rays recommendations easier to judge.
